author: ohtadmin
title: Playground at Head's Beach proposed
text:
A proposal to install a playground at Head’s Beach has taken its first swing toward fruition.
The director of parks and recreation, Ray DeFalco, was authorized to apply for a $125,000 grant through the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management. The aim is “to expand recreation opportunities for families on the north end” by constructing “a small, inclusive playground for children ages 3-5.”
DeFalco also was authorized to apply for a $261,000 grant to expand the existing playground on North Road. This proposal features fully accessible restrooms, security cameras, solar-powered Big-belly trash cans and musical instruments from Freenotes Harmony Park.
The councilors approved both requests at their Nov. 3 meeting. The grants would require matching dollars of $30,000 and $65,000, respectively.
The project on North Road received unanimous approval from President Nancy Beye, Vice President Erik Brine and Councilwomen Mary Glackin and Mary Meagher. Councilman Eddie Ross was absent.
“I’m delighted there would be a bathroom at the playground,” Meagher said. “I’m absolutely thrilled with that. … This is absolutely essential.”
The proposal for Head’s Beach, however, had a dissenter, Beye, who said “it doesn’t make sense to me.” Concerned with parking, liability, overcrowding and maintenance, she was irked about the application being “all of sudden” scheduled for a vote without time to vet those apprehensions.
“I just don’t think we need to duplicate our playground,” she said.
Meagher asked Beye if her issue was applying for the grant without vetting her concerns.
“The cart is a little before the horse?” Meagher asked. “Is that what you’re saying?”
“Yes,” Beye replied. “I don’t think we’re at that point yet.”
Brine, however, said the council should not miss any opportunities to win money.
“I entirely get what you’re saying,” he told Beye, “but I just don’t want to miss the opportunity to spend state money in Jamestown. I agree, I would love to know more and get community feedback. But I think it is important that we submit these grants so we have the opportunity to get some more state resources.”
Brine said not applying for these grants is “negligent.”
“This is something we should apply for every single time,” he said. “I’m not saying that specifically for this project. This isn’t the first thing I would fund, personally, by any means. This is funding that could go to Eldred Field. This is funding that could go to Fort Getty. But we have enough infrastructure needs that every time this grant application comes up, we should submit.”
Charlotte Zarlengo, of Seaside Drive, said she had safety concerns regarding a playground at Head’s Beach.
“This would be 20 feet from the water,” she said. “Children love to play and run around. That body of water is such an attraction to everybody, especially to young children who have no idea how dangerous it can be. The thought of putting a playground that close to the water is unbelievable. It is a very, very bad spot.”
Mello, however, said “it’s not unusual for playgrounds to be associated with waterfronts and beaches.” DeFalco and Meagher said keeping children away from the water was the job of their parents.
“I understand what you’re saying,” Meagher told Zarlengo, “but we rely on people to actually watch their kids. And we rely on the wisdom of children to stay out of the water.”
“It’s up to parents to watch their kids,” DeFalco said.
Glackin, whose children visit Head’s Beach, said a playground would give kids in the neighborhood something to do besides “playing on the jetty or hanging onto the one tree that’s down there.” A playground, moreover, would help get kids away from video games. “To have a place for kids to go, where they can ride their bikes to, is really important,” she said. “It’s not that I don’t have a swing in my yard or a trampoline somewhere. It’s about getting out of the house. It’s being a little bit independent in a safe space.”
Mike Moratta, of Sampan Avenue, agreed.
“There’s no reason why anyone in the Shores shouldn’t be able to walk safely into a playground, and walking to a playground at Head’s Beach is perfect,” he said. “You’re equidistant to basically everyone in the Shores. You don’t have to traverse main roads with no sidewalks. It’s a great loop to take the family.”
Moratta, moreover, said a playground would help his 2-year-old daughter meet friends in her neighborhood.
“They can forge the friendships that create the community Jamestown is known for,” he said.
DeFalco said the state is not “super strict” about the specific elements in the applications. While his application calls for musical instruments from Freenotes Harmony Park, any “music-related accessibility features” could be considered at the next step of the process. Town Administrator Ed Mello called these applications “very high level.”
“We have a long way to go in terms of vetting the process,” he said. “There is a long process ahead.”
“Even if these applications don’t necessarily pass because they don’t have all the details, every time we apply and we don’t get it, it makes us more eligible and likely to get it in the next time,” Brine said. “If we don’t apply, we’re not getting that benefit.”
